name: Thiamidol

lead: Thiamidol is a synthetic compound in over-the-counter serums and creams that fade dark spots, melasma and post-acne marks. It was designed to block human tyrosinase, the enzyme that starts melanin production, so less pigment is made.

It was identified by screening about 50,000 compounds against human tyrosinase rather than the mushroom enzyme used in much earlier lightener research. Several randomized trials, some comparing 0.2% thiamidol with 4% hydroquinone or a vehicle, have reported improvement in hyperpigmentation; many tested branded products and are industry-linked.

paras: People use it as a daily serum or cream on dark spots or the whole face, usually with sunscreen, and report gradual fading over weeks to months.
The trials assessed tolerability alongside efficacy, and adverse-event rates are not detailed in the sources reviewed. Long-term and independent comparative data are limited.

angle.text: Thiamidol blocks the tyrosinase enzyme so less melanin is made, fading dark spots, post-inflammatory marks and melasma in over-the-counter serums. Several randomized trials of 0.2% formulations exist, though most are industry-linked.

lead: Thiamidol (isobutylamido thiazolyl resorcinol) is a synthetic resorcinol-derived compound developed as an inhibitor of human tyrosinase, the rate-limiting enzyme of melanin production. It is used in over-the-counter cosmetic serums and creams aimed at dark spots, post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation and melasma.[1][2]

It was identified by screening a library of about 50,000 compounds against recombinant human tyrosinase rather than the mushroom tyrosinase used in much earlier lightener research. The authors of that screen reported that many earlier whitening ingredients had been identified using the mushroom enzyme and differ in how they interact with the human one.[1]

Published human studies, mostly randomized split-face or parallel-group trials of 0.2% formulations in melasma and post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation, are discussed below. A dermatology review of cosmeceuticals for facial hyperpigmentation also covers it among newer options.[3][4][5][6][7]

paras: Thiamidol is designed to block human tyrosinase, the enzyme that catalyzes the early steps of melanin synthesis. In the screening study, researchers compared hits from a 50,000-compound library, tested on recombinant human tyrosinase, with established lightening agents including hydroquinone, and reported that inhibitors of human tyrosinase needed molecular motifs different from those of mushroom tyrosinase inhibitors.[1]

Later chemistry papers on resorcinol-containing compounds describe the resorcinol motif as a recurring feature of potent human tyrosinase inhibitors and have explored related structures in cell models.[8][9]

An exploratory double-blind, randomized split-face study in women with mild to moderate melasma compared thiamidol with hydroquinone; its authors reported significant improvement of melasma with thiamidol.[3]

A 2021 evaluator-blinded randomized trial of 50 women with facial melasma compared 0.2% thiamidol with 4% hydroquinone cream over a period in late 2020, assessing efficacy and tolerability.[4] A 24-week randomized, double-blind, vehicle-controlled study in moderate-to-severe melasma also included a subsequent regression phase after treatment stopped.[7]

A 2021 study reported reduced post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation with a thiamidol regimen,[5] and an international multi-centre program combined a double-blind split-face study with an open-label real-world study in facial hyperpigmentation.[6] ClinicalTrials.gov lists a completed 200-participant trial of a 0.2% cream for facial hyperpigmentation[10] and a completed study of a brand skincare routine in post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation.[11]
Many of these studies were of branded formulations and several were sponsored by or connected to the product developers; independent long-term comparative data are limited.

Thiamidol is promoted in mainstream skincare as a hydroquinone-free alternative for dark spots. Reviews of pigment treatments describe hydroquinone as a long-standing standard whose use is restricted or debated in some jurisdictions, which is the context in which newer inhibitors are discussed.[12]

timeline.event: Human-tyrosinase screening of 50,000 compounds is published, describing the discovery approach.[1]
Split-face melasma study versus hydroquinone published.[3]
Randomized trials versus 4% hydroquinone and vehicle, and a post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation study, are published.[4][5][7]
